messages.author: fd4f3538f907404b
messages.subject: too many questions about Lambert W function in TMB
parts:
I have an application (functional responses in a predator-prey
system with depletion) for which the predicted value involves the
result of a Lambert W function
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambert_W_function>. (I only need this
for positive real inputs, so there's no messing around with
complex-valued or multi-valued functions.)

It's not too hard to write C++ code to compute W(z) (in fact there's
already some code in the TMB codebase for this, in the one-step-ahead
residual computation), but all of the ways I know to compute this are
iterative, which means that they will involve if() statements, even
though the final output is continuous (at least as far as it can be in
floating-point).

I *think* this means that I need to define a new "primitive" (the
term in adcomp seems to be "atomic"?) function to tell TMB that W(z)
has a specified derivative W'(z) [maybe I also need to define W''(z)]
? So far I haven't been able to find any examples/documentation of
how I would do this ...

By analogy with ADMB (chapter 13 of the the manual), I need to write
new adjoint code. The TODO file for the adcomp package
https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/master/TODO.md includes 'Make
simple example of how to include "adjoint code". pexp(x,lambda) is a
good example (cum. dist. function exp. distr)'
(I poked around looking for pexp, but it seems that right now the
implementation uses a CppAD function ...)

* Does my diagnosis seem right?
* Where should I start looking for documentation or examples?
* Any chance someone's done this (written atomic/adjoint code for
the Lambert W function in TMB) already?

parts:
You're right Ben. This can be handled with 'atomic functions'. The Lambert W function is a great example which should be put in the manual. Here's a first pass:

#include <TMB.hpp>

// Step 1: Code up a plain C version
double W(double x) {
  double reltol = 1.490116e-08;
  double logx = log(x);
  double y = (logx > 0 ? logx : 0);
  int niter = 100;
  int i=0;
  for (; i < niter; i++) {
    if ( fabs( logx - log(y) - y) < reltol) break;
    double fdivg = (y - exp(logx - y)) / (1 + y);
    y = y - fdivg;
  }
  if (i == niter) Rf_warning("W: failed convergence");
  return y;
}

// Step 2: Code up reverse mode derivatives:
// x = W(x) * exp( W(x) )
// W'(x) = 1 / ( exp(W(x)) * (1 + W(x)) )
TMB_ATOMIC_VECTOR_FUNCTION(
               // ATOMIC_NAME
               W
               ,
               // OUTPUT_DIM
               1,
               // ATOMIC_DOUBLE
               double x = tx[0]; // input
                           ty[0] = W(x);     // output
               ,
               // ATOMIC_REVERSE
               Type W = ty[0];   // Function value
               px[0] = 1. / (exp(W) * (1. + W)) * py[0];
               )

// Step 3: Make version with scalar arguments:
template<class Type>
Type W(Type x){
  CppAD::vector<Type> tx(1);
  tx[0] = x;
  return W(tx)[0];
}

template<class Type>
Type objective_function<Type>::operator() ()
{
  PARAMETER(x);
  Type f = W(x);
  return f;
}

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Re: too many questions about Lambert W function in TMB
parts:
wow! thanks! there's so much in here that, while reasonably easy to
understand once you've done it for me, would have taken days to figure
out for myself. Let me know if you want assistance in writing up the
explanation of this in a way that will be comprehensible to a newbie
like myself ...

FWIW more efficient iterative special-purpose algorithms to compute
Lambert-W exist, but I think Newton's method will work just fine. (If
I get ambitious maybe I'll try to use your example as a template to
code one of them up: I don't think I'd have to do anything but replace
the body of the plain-C++ code ...)

cheers
Ben Bolker
